analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to pay property owners when regulation lowers their property's value, and makes takings lawsuits easier to file.
analysis.headline: The Property Rights Litigation Relief Act of 1995, introduced by Senator Hatch with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal — and, for federally mandated programs, state — agencies to compensate owners whenever a government action physically invaded property, blocked its use, or cut its value by 20% (or $10,000) or more. It would have let owners sue in either federal district court or the Court of Federal Claims, waived the government's sovereign immunity, put the burden of proof on the government in most cases, and awarded attorney's fees to winning property owners. Compensation could include business losses and interest. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote, and it died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners whose land or business value was reduced by federal or federally-driven state regulation — most consequentially large landholders and developers, since only owners with sizable value at stake could afford to litigate. The bill would also have benefited the litigation and appraisal industries through a new stream of takings claims, fees, and valuations.

how_it_helps.text: It would have required federal agencies to pay owners whenever an action physically invades property, blocks nearly all beneficial use, exacts property as a permit condition without rough proportionality, fails to substantially advance a stated government interest, or cuts the property's value by 20% (or $10,000) or more.

It would have let owners sue in either federal district court or the Court of Federal Claims, ending the current choice between getting an injunction in one court or money in the other, and repealed the rule barring simultaneous suits.

It put the burden of proof on the government for most categories of claim, waived federal sovereign immunity, allowed attorney's fees for prevailing property owners, and let compensation include business losses and compounded interest.
It would have made states enforcing federally mandated regulatory programs liable to pay compensation, on the theory that the federal government should bear the cost of programs it requires.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through agency budgets and the Judgment Fund, which would bear compensation payments, business-loss awards, interest, and attorney's fees. The public would also bear the cost of environmental, land-use, and health-and-safety protections that became far more expensive to enforce once nearly every value-reducing action triggered a payable claim.

drawbacks.text: The bill required compensation whenever a federal action lowered a property's value by 20% or more (or by $10,000 or more) — a threshold far broader than the Supreme Court's takings doctrine, which historically required near-total loss of use. Critics in the 1990s warned such statutes could make ordinary zoning, wetlands, and endangered-species protections financially prohibitive, effectively requiring taxpayers to buy out every significant restriction.

It shifted the burden of proof to the government to justify many land-use conditions and to prove a use is a nuisance, which defenders of regulation argued would let property owners escape health, safety, and environmental rules by claiming payment, and would chill agencies from enforcing standards at all.

The bill covered not only federal agencies but state agencies carrying out federally mandated programs, raising federalism concerns and exposing states' federally-related regulatory programs to compensation claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had genuine strengths: it would have fixed real procedural traps that forced property owners to choose between courts and could not win complete relief in either. But its compensation triggers were sweeping — a 20% (or $10,000) drop in value triggered payment even when the regulation stayed in force, and compensation included business losses — which would have converted much routine environmental, land-use, and safety regulation into a payable claim. Critics of such proposals have long argued they let a regulated party pay a fee to pollute or build rather than comply, shifting public burdens onto taxpayers. A well-designed takings-process fix would have separated the two goals; this bill combined them, and it never advanced far enough to be revised.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Hatch introduced it on the opening day of the 104th Congress, it was sent to the Judiciary Committee, and nothing further happened before Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced January 4, 1995 and read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
The only recorded action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks on November 27, 1995; the committee never held a markup and the Senate never voted.
The 104th Congress ended January 3, 1997 without the bill receiving any vote, so it died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal regulatory agencies and the treasury kept the status quo: no new compensation obligations and no new litigation exposure. Owners seeking compensation for regulatory losses gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in November 1995.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no party split can be measured; the bill was a single Republican senator's initiative that never advanced.

industries.industry: Landowners, developers, and resource interests (real estate, mining, timber, agriculture)
industries.note: The bill would have made the federal government pay whenever regulation cut property value by 20% or more or blocked its use, and would have made suits easier to file and win, with attorney's fees included. Only large landholders with valuable affected parcels were realistically positioned to litigate these claims.

industries.industry: Federal regulatory agencies (environmental, land management, health and safety)
industries.note: Agencies would have faced new compensation liability, shifted burdens of proof, and budgetary exposure for compensation paid from their own appropriations — increasing the cost of issuing protective rules.
A new category of federal takings litigation, with fee-shifting, expert testimony, and optional AAA-style arbitration, would have generated substantial legal and appraisal work.
